what_its_for: Calcitriol is a form of Vitamin D that your body needs to absorb calcium and keep your bones strong. Doctors prescribe it to treat low calcium levels in the blood, weak or soft bones, and problems with your parathyroid glands (small glands in your neck that control calcium). It is also used in people with kidney disease who cannot make enough Vitamin D on their own.
how_to_take: Take calcitriol capsules or liquid by mouth exactly as your doctor tells you. You can take it with or without food. If you are using the liquid form, measure your dose carefully with the dropper that comes with it — do not use a kitchen spoon. If your doctor prescribed the topical (skin) ointment form (Vectical), apply a thin layer only to the affected skin area and wash your hands well after use. Do not swallow the ointment. Take this medicine at the same time each day to help you remember.
dosing: Your dose will be set by your doctor based on your condition, your calcium and vitamin D blood levels, and how your kidneys work. A common starting dose for adults is 0.25 micrograms (mcg) once a day, and your doctor may slowly increase it. Your doctor will do regular blood tests to check your calcium levels and adjust your dose as needed. Never change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next scheduled dose, skip the missed dose and continue your regular schedule. Do not take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one, as this could raise your calcium to a dangerous level.
storage: Store calcitriol capsules and liquid at room temperature, between 59°F and 77°F (15°C and 25°C). Keep it away from heat, direct sunlight, and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep the bottle tightly closed. Store the ointment at room temperature and do not freeze it. Keep all forms of this medicine out of reach of children and pets.
what_to_avoid: Avoid taking extra Vitamin D supplements or calcium supplements unless your doctor specifically tells you to, because calcitriol already increases the amount of calcium in your body and too much can be harmful. Avoid foods very high in calcium (like large amounts of dairy) unless your doctor says it is okay. Do not take antacids that contain magnesium (like Maalox or Mylanta) while on calcitriol without asking your doctor first. Avoid getting dehydrated. Tell all your healthcare providers, including your pharmacist, about every vitamin, supplement, and medicine you take.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience signs of too much calcium (high calcium levels), such as: nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, stomach pain, constipation, feeling very thirsty, urinating more than usual, unusual tiredness or weakness, confusion, muscle weakness, bone pain, or irregular heartbeat. Also contact your doctor if you develop headaches, dizziness, ringing in the ears, or any new or unusual symptoms. Do not stop taking calcitriol without talking to your doctor first.
when_it_works: Calcitriol starts working within a few hours of your first dose, but you may not feel a noticeable difference right away. It may take several weeks of regular use before your calcium levels are fully balanced and your symptoms improve. Your doctor will check your blood and urine regularly to make sure the medicine is working properly and your calcium levels are safe.
special_populations: Kidney disease: Calcitriol is often prescribed specifically for people with chronic kidney disease, but your dose must be carefully managed and monitored. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, as this medicine may affect your baby. Children: Doses for children are based on body weight and age — always follow your doctor's exact instructions. Older adults: Older adults may be more sensitive to high calcium levels and should be monitored closely. Always tell your doctor about all your medical conditions before starting calcitriol.
